item.title: Solved: How to Prevent Class Data from Being Shared Among Instances
item.description:
When working with classes in Python, it is common to run into the issue of instance data being unintentionally shared between different instances. This behavior can lead to surprising results where changes in one instance affect another. Let’s take a closer look at how we can prevent this unwanted sharing and ensure each instance maintains its own separate data.

Consider the following behavior:

class A:
    shared_list = []

x = A()
y = A()

x.shared_list.append(1)
y.shared_list.append(2)
x.shared_list.append(3)
y.shared_list.append(4)

print(x.shared_list)  # Output: [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(y.shared_list)  # Output: [1, 2, 3, 4]

This code demonstrates that both x and y share the same class attribute shared_list. When we append items to this list from either instance, it modifies the same underlying data structure, leading to the output indicating the shared nature of the list: [1, 2, 3, 4].

item.title: Solved: Why Superclass __init__ Methods Aren't Automatically Invoked in Python
item.description:
Why did the designers of Python choose not to automatically invoke the __init__() methods of a subclass’s superclass? For those familiar with other programming languages, this can be a point of confusion. Here, we will explore this design choice and understand the recommended idiomatic approach to class initialization in Python.

Understanding the Design Choice

In many programming languages, it is common for subclass constructors to automatically call their superclass constructors. However, Python takes a different path. The rationale behind this choice is primarily rooted in flexibility. When you define a subclass, the parameters you need may differ significantly from those required by the superclass’s constructor, which complicates automatic calls.
